Summary (auto):
Weekly POC sync focused on cost/unit economics. Reviewed tokens/sec per dollar benchmarks, impact of prefix/KV caching, and tradeoffs when increasing batch sizes. Agreed next steps: run extended benchmark with 8k context, share updated cost spreadsheet, and security to review SOC2 appendix.

Topics: tokens/sec/$, caching savings, batching tradeoffs, memory/kv cache hit rates, quantization effects, dedicated vs hosted pricing considerations, network egress, SSO and audit logs.

Transcript:
00:00 Lena: ok good morning everybody uh thanks for joining, we'll do a quick agenda - cost review, tuning notes, and next steps. Marcus you got the numbers?
00:15 Marcus: yeah I put together the baseline from last week's runs — so to reiterate baseline is hosted small instance using gtx-ish VMs, we saw about 1,200 tokens per second at p50 but cost per 1M tokens was high because there was no effective prefix caching, so net tokens per dollar ended up around 18k tokens per dollar.
00:35 Priya: wait when you say prefix caching are you talking about the K V cache or the prefix cache? sometimes the tooling names get swapped.
00:45 Marcus: yeah it's the KV cache, sorry I sometimes say K V. It's the prefix/KV cache that avoids re-computing encoder past tokens for repeated prompts like our triage templates. Hit rate was variable — roughly 60% on average for our sample traffic.
01:05 Samir: so that 60% hit rate — that reduces tokens emitted to the model or reduces compute? I need to understand which line item I'm reducing on the cost sheet.
01:15 Marcus: good question — it reduces compute cycles because the runtime can reuse the KV cache, so fewer forward passes. On the spreadsheet we model it as effective tokens served decreased (so tokens/sec per dollar increases) since same endpoint serves more logical tokens with same flops.
01:30 Priya: ok and what about batching? we tried batch size 8 last week but saw p95 latency spike — is that still acceptable for our SLA?
01:40 Marcus: tradeoff there — larger batch sizes give cheaper tokens/sec because of GPU utilization, but tail latency suffers. For our use case with clinical chat the p95 target is 300ms for short queries; with batch8 we were at 650ms p95. Batch size 4 was a nicer middle ground — tokens/sec dropped a bit but p95 sat at about 320-350ms.
02:05 Elena: anything on encryption and KMS usage? if we enable KMS there's overhead, right? I recall earlier conversation about HSM-backed keys increasing latency for some requests.
02:15 Marcus: encryption at rest and envelope encryption via KMS adds minimal latency to token generation path; the main impact is on key management calls during startup or key rotation. For in-flight path we keep keys cached — the extra overhead is in setup not per-token. HSM-backed signing might add tiny ms at handshake but not per request token generation unless you're doing per-token signing which you aren't.
02:40 Lena: let's go through the cost spreadsheet quick — I highlighted three scenarios: hosted baseline (no cache), hosted w/ cache, dedicated reserved capacity with 99th percentile SLA. The numbers assume our quantized model profile Q4 (8-bit) which gives about 1.8x tokens/sec vs fp16 but varies with seq length.
03:05 Marcus: right sequence length matters — at 512 tokens the advantage is bigger; at 8k context the kernel selection changes, performance drops somewhat. In the spreadsheet I included a column for tokens/sec at 512, 2048, and 8192 contexts.
03:20 Priya: the 8k context is core to our triage pipeline — we need embeddings + long context recall so those numbers are critical.
03:28 Marcus: agreed, that's why we proposed the extended benchmark: 1 hour run at production QPS with 8k contexts, measure KV cache hit rate, GPU utilization, actual tokens/sec and tokens per dollar.
03:42 Noah: can you remind us how tokens per dollar is computed? I want to show product team the delta if caching improves.
03:50 Lena: sure — it's model throughput (tokens/sec) times seconds in month, divided by monthly infra cost for that config. We also model effective logical tokens saved from cache as increasing tokens/sec because the same hardware serves more logical requests. We include network egress and storage overhead in a separate tab.
04:10 Samir: for our infra planning, are you assuming burstable GPU pools or fixed reserved capacity? that changes monthly cost a lot.
04:20 Lena: scenarios include both. Dedicated reserved is higher fixed cost but predictable tokens/sec and SLOs; hosted is usage-based and cheaper for low QPS but can get expensive at scale. There's also burst-to-dedicated option in the doc for seasonal spikes.
04:35 Elena: security question — will logs include PII? we need audit logs but must ensure no PHI in plain text off-cluster.
04:45 Marcus: logs are configurable; the default is redacted transcript logs. We can stream audit logs to your SIEM; Redwood Private deployment can be set up to keep data in your VPC so nothing leaves your network.
04:58 Priya: earlier you mentioned quantization tradeoffs — how much quality drop do you see at 8-bit for our tasks?
05:10 Marcus: in our internal eval we saw small delta on generative wording but for extraction tasks like triage it was within tolerance. We'll attach eval prompt-sets. We also support mixed precision so we can run critical layers in fp16 and rest in 8-bit.
05:30 Lena: ok back to numbers — Marcus can you talk through the cached vs uncached tokens/sec/$ at our observed hit rate?
05:40 Marcus: with 60% hit rate our tokens per dollar jumps from ~18k to ~38k in hosted baseline. If hit rate hits 80% it goes to ~55k. Dedicated reserved improves raw tokens/sec so per-dollar improves further, but remember commit cost up-front. The spreadsheet shows break-even at around 2.2M monthly active tokens for reserved to be cheaper.
06:05 Samir: is that 2.2M logical tokens or raw tokens? we need clarity.
06:10 Marcus: logical tokens — after caching. Raw model tokens are higher but billed depends on infra in reserved path; we tried to show both columns.
06:20 Priya: any thoughts on adaptive batching? where small queries bypass batching for latency-sensitive and bulk ops go into larger batches.
06:30 Marcus: yes that's in the routing section — you can have two pools: low-latency pool with smaller batch sizes and a throughput pool; the router splits by route and priority. That adds complexity but gets the best of both worlds.
06:45 Noah: does that require dedicated capacity to be effective?
06:50 Marcus: not necessarily but dedicated gives more predictable behaviour; hosted can do it too but you'll see variable tail depending on noisy neighbors.
07:00 Lena: let's capture decisions: run extended 8k benchmark, Marcus will instrument KV cache hit rate, we will update cost sheet and re-run sensitivity for 60/80/95% cache hits, security sends SOC2 appendix.
07:12 Elena: quick question about audit retention — is retention configurable per route? we need 7-year retention for some logs.
07:20 Marcus: retention is configurable in Redwood Private; hosted supports configurable retention tiers but long-term archivals might need dedicated log export to your storage.
07:30 Priya: anything on rate limiting or quotas we should be aware of that affect tokens/sec?
07:38 Jamie: we have token-level throttles, per-route quotas, and reservoir bursting rules. You'll want to tune those during pilot to match your SLA.
07:52 Samir: one more ops note — our infra team will want the raw GPU metrics you collect for benchmarking. Can you provide exported prometheus format?
08:00 Marcus: yes I'll upload prom metrics and raw logs from the run.
08:05 Lena: ok timing — Marcus will kick off the 1-hour run this week, upload results, Lena will update the cost sheet, security appendix goes to Elena by Monday. Any objections?
08:18 Priya: none. Sounds good.
08:22 Noah: quick pricing question — if we go dedicated reserved what's the typical commit term?
08:28 Lena: usually annual or 12-month with options for monthly billing for burst capacity. We'll propose a 12-month sizing in the next call.
08:36 Elena: for SOC2 and network diagrams — I'll review once you send them.
08:40 Lena: great, thanks everyone. We'll recap next steps in the email.
